planting.note: Sow fresh acorns 1 inch deep in fall directly where the tree is to grow, since the long taproot resents transplanting once established.

directions: Coast Live Oak is the iconic evergreen oak of California's coastal ranges, forming a broad, dense, often wider-than-tall canopy of stiff, holly-like leaves over a massive, gnarled trunk. It is a keystone species of California oak woodland, supporting acorn woodpeckers, scrub jays, and dozens of other wildlife species, and is famously intolerant of summer irrigation, which encourages fatal Phytophthora root disease. Give it lean, well-drained soil and withhold water beneath the drip line once established, and it will live for centuries with essentially no care. Its slow growth and enormous mature size reward gardeners planting for the long term rather than quick shade.

planting.note: Sow fresh acorns 1 inch deep in fall in rocky, sharply drained soil; this species handles poor, shallow soils better than most oaks.

directions: Canyon Live Oak takes its common name from the steep, rocky canyons and cliff faces of the western mountains where it grows, and its species name from the fuzzy, golden-scaled acorn cup that distinguishes it from every other western oak. It is remarkably variable in form, growing as a tall forest tree in moist canyons but hugging the ground as a wind-sculpted shrub on exposed ridges and serpentine outcrops, and it tolerates poorer, thinner soils than Coast Live Oak. Its dense, extremely hard wood was historically split into mauls and tool handles, and its abundant acorns are a major wildlife food source across a huge elevational range from Oregon to Baja California. Choose it for rocky slopes, dry canyons, or poor soils where few other trees will establish.
sources: USDA Forest Service Fire Effects Information System

planting.note: Sow fresh acorns 1 inch deep in fall into well-drained foothill soil; young trees establish a deep taproot quickly and resent later transplanting.

directions: Interior Live Oak replaces Coast Live Oak in California's hot, dry inland valleys and Sierra Nevada foothills, where it forms dense woodlands alongside Blue Oak and Gray Pine on thin, rocky, summer-baked soils. Its glossy, convex, holly-shaped leaves curl slightly and reflect sunlight, an adaptation to the intense heat of its interior range, and mature trees develop a dark, dense, rounded canopy that provides critical shade and acorn forage for deer and birds in otherwise open foothill grassland. It is markedly more heat- and drought-tolerant than the coastal species and better suited to hot interior gardens with alkaline or decomposed-granite soils. Plant it where nothing else will thrive on a hot, dry slope and expect a long-lived, low-maintenance shade tree.
sources: USDA Forest Service Fire Effects Information System

planting.note: Sow fresh acorns 1 inch deep in fall in lean, well-drained chaparral soil; established plants need no irrigation and resent summer water.

directions: California Scrub Oak is the dominant shrub of chaparral plant communities across the California coast ranges and foothills, forming dense, spiny-leaved thickets that were once misidentified as a shrub form of Coast Live Oak before being recognized as their own species. Unlike its tree-form relatives, it stays a manageable multi-stemmed shrub, resprouting vigorously from a stout basal burl after fire and forming impenetrable wildlife cover that shelters quail, rabbits, and songbirds. Its acorns are smaller but no less valuable to wildlife than those of larger oaks, and its dense evergreen structure makes it a superior choice for a low-water native screening hedge or slope stabilization planting where a full-size oak would be too large. It thrives on neglect once established and is an excellent substitute for non-native evergreen shrubs in a fire-wise landscape.
